newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr rise ebbs from 115 yen on officials' remarks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr rise ebbs from 115 yen on officials' remarks.

text.p: The dollar's gain against the yen temporarily ebbed by late Thursday in Tokyo as Japanese officials signalled they did not want an excessive dollar rise that might hurt Japan's economy and stock market, dealers said.
The greenback topped the 115 yen level and clawed as high as 115.12 yen in the morning, its highest in over 44 months.
"What we saw here was selling of Japanese assets (of the yen, stocks and bonds)," said Kazunori Iida, manager at the foreign exchange department of Nissho Iwai Corp.
The benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares briefly dropped as low as 18,819.92, the first time it had been below the key 19,000 level since December 6, 1995.
It clawed up by late trade to end down 257.83 points at 19,291.58.
"Given the fragile stock market and the dollar's strength, there is a fear that overseas players may accelerate the shifting of their assets out of Japan," Iida added.
Iida said it seemed financial markets were issuing a warning to the government that Japan's economy next year would not be as good as the authorities believed.
A senior Finance Ministry official said on Thursday that Japan's monetary authorities do not welcome wild currency fluctuations and were keeping a close watch on currency developments.

A senior Bank of Japan (BOJ) official also echoed some of his comments. "Regarding recent developments in the foreign exchange market, we are adequately and carefully monitoring the market," the official told Reuters.

Analysts and dealers said Japan's monetary authorities were worried about excessive weakness of the yen beyond 115 yen because they thought such a movement was out of line with economic fundamentals and would harm Japan's economy.
The dollar was relatively well-bid at around 114.50 yen in late trade even after the comments by the Japanese officials, dealers said.

"These comments may temporarily put a lid on the dollar's rise but may not be able to reverse the trend of the dollar's further rise on a longer-term basis," said a dealer at a long-term credit bank in Tokyo.

Dealers said the dollar's gains in the early morning were not overdone since there were still lots of operators such as oil importers who needed to buy dollars and interbank traders had not established excessive dollar long positions.

"Dollar buying in the past few days was mainly related to settlements of oil imports, individuals' travelling overseas and repatriation of profits by foreign firms in Japan ahead of the year-end," said the long-term credit bank dealer.
Dealers said even after these seasonal dollar buying factors wane, a lack of yen buying factors is likely to keep the dollar firm against the yen next year.
Nissho Iwai's Iida said the U.S. currency was likely to rise to 116 or 117 yen but expected to stay around there for a while.
The dollar/mark trade was thin on Boxing Day with nearly no participation from European institutions, dealers in Singapore said.
"Usually there is a correlation between a strong dollar/yen to dollar/mark, but we're not seeing the full impact as Europe is mostly on holiday," a Singapore bank dealer said.
